reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .364 xwOBA and .484 xSLG tell you the damage is genuine, and 41 projected home runs with 38 stolen bases is a combination that almost no player in baseball can threaten. The Statcast profile shows why: a 12.8% barrel rate and 48.8% hard-hit rate from a guy running 29.5 ft/s, which means every ball in play carries a secondary threat that most power hitters simply cannot add. The one honest complication is a 34.2% chase rate that produces a 26.2% strikeout rate — the walk rate at 11.7% holds the line for now, keeping that .369 projected OBP livable, but if pitchers find a way to exploit the zone-expanding tendencies, the contact floor gets exposed fast. At 24, with this kind of speed-power blend already showing up in the underlying numbers, the ceiling in the projection isn't hypothetical.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-three home runs projected from a 23-year-old third baseman with a 93.0 mph average exit velocity and 50.4% hard-hit rate is not a stretch — the contact quality is there to support it. The Statcast profile is almost entirely about what happens when he puts the bat on the ball: xwOBA at .364 and xSLG at .493 both sit near the top of the league, and his 11.7% walk rate gives the line a real on-base floor. The read hinges on the strikeout suppression holding, because 18.0% is manageable now, but his whiff rate is middling, and if pitchers find a consistent exploit there the counting stats compress fast. If the contact quality translates cleanly across 702 plate appearances, Caminero is a legitimate middle-of-the-order force regardless of what the rest of his game is, and the rest of his game, including defense, gives you little reason for comfort beyond the bat.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact profile and the contact results don't quite match, and that gap is the whole argument. De La Cruz's 93.8 mph average exit velocity sits at the 98th percentile, his hard-hit rate is 50.8%, and yet a 27.0% strikeout rate drags the actual batting line below what the batted-ball shape deserves — the .274 xBA and .361 xwOBA are both cleaner than anything he's produced on paper. The projection splits the difference: .268/.347/.475 across 638 PA, 26 home runs, 30 stolen bases, the kind of counting-stat line that plays even if the swing-and-miss never fully resolves. The whole profile hinges on whether the 27.7% whiff rate stays stable or creeps; if pitchers continue to find the zone against him and the strikeout rate climbs, the power and speed still produce value, just less of it than the exit-velocity profile implies he should be giving you.

reports.name: Jackson Chourio
reports.published_report: The power contact profile is legitimate at 91.9 mph average exit velocity and a 13.3% barrel rate, but the chase rate tells a different story. At 34.2%, he's expanding the zone at a level that caps his walk rate at 8.1% and keeps the strikeout rate at 23.7%, which is why the xBA (.259) lands so far below the xSLG (.480). The projection at .279/.339/.476 with 25 home runs essentially says the bat speed carries him past the discipline problem, and for now it does. If pitchers learn to live on the edges and he never tightens that chase number, the floor is a guy with real pop but a low-.330s OBP who's interesting but not quite the sum of his tools.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The 33-homer projection carries a quiet tension: the Statcast profile that supports it is more contact-shape than raw-power story. His xSLG sits at .431 in current MLB data, which is above average but not the number you'd expect to back a slugger's line, and his barrel rate of 9.8% and average exit velocity of 89.4 mph are both right around the middle of the league. What's happening is that his sprint speed, 28.5 ft/s at the 80th percentile, is doing real work, turning gap contact into extra bases and 31 projected stolen bases into genuine run value. The profile hinges on plate discipline: a 36.8% chase rate in the bottom sixth of the league is the ceiling suppressor, and if that doesn't improve, the .341 projected OBP starts looking generous and the whole offensive case gets thinner. When the contact and the speed work together, you're looking at a legitimate top-of-the-order everyday shortstop; if the chase rate stays where it is, he's a high-upside version of a second-division regular.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins

At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The Statcast profile explains the rest of him: a 12.6% strikeout rate that puts him in genuinely elite contact territory, paired with an 87.3 mph average exit velocity and a 4.5% barrel rate that sit near the bottom of the league, which is why the xwOBA lands at .316 and the xSLG at .387 despite all that bat-to-ball skill. He's a contact-over-power first baseman with real speed, and the profile works as long as that contact quality translates to enough value to cover a glaring lack of thump at the position. If the speed projection holds and the strikeout rate stays where it is, he's a productive, useful everyday player; if the exit velocity profile means the barrel rate can't improve, he's a low-average-power first baseman that a team tolerates rather than builds around.

reports.name: William Contreras

Contreras pairs that discipline with a .441 xSLG and 43.8% hard-hit rate that say the projected .405 SLG is a touch conservative rather than a stretch. The whole profile reads as a catcher who handles the bat better than the raw power numbers suggest, with league-average walk rates doing nothing to hurt him. If there's a dependency here, it's whether the .271 AVG projection actually catches up to a .263 xBA, because a guy this easy to put in the lineup every day at catcher doesn't need much more than that to be genuinely valuable.

reports.name: Bo Bichette
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is the gap between what he does with contact and what he does with his eyes. A 41.1% chase rate lands in the 4th percentile, and yet an 87th-percentile xBA of .276 says the contact itself is genuinely good, good enough that he keeps getting hits even while swinging at nearly everything outside the zone. The .412 xSLG is decent without being scary, the barrel rate sits at 6.3%, and the projection's .703 OPS reflects a player whose discipline is costing him real offensive ground, not a player who's somehow masking bad contact. If he ever tightens the zone even modestly, there's a useful everyday shortstop here; if the chase rate stays where it is, he's a second-division regular who bats .263 and gives you 17 home runs in 687 plate appearances, no more.

reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report: A 4.3% strikeout rate is the whole profile. Contact so consistent that his 7.7% whiff rate sits at the 100th percentile, and an xBA of .291 backs up why a .315 projected average across 673 plate appearances is plausible even though his 86.4 mph exit velocity and 1.2% barrel rate are about as far from a power threat as you'll find in the big leagues. reports.name: Bryce Miller

The tension is that his 24.5% strikeout rate and 25.8% whiff rate suggest the chase isn't always converting into a punchout: he's getting batters to expand but not always punishing them for it, which is what separates a mid-rotation workhorse from a difference-maker. Reynolds hits the ball hard on a consistent basis, 46.7% hard-hit rate, but something in the contact shape bleeds exit velocity into outs rather than extra bases, which is why the xBA lands at .247 while the xwOBA reads 80th percentile. At 703 projected PA, the .365 OBP is the real asset, a patient loud-contact profile that delivers run-scoring value even when the hit rate disappoints. He's a solid everyday outfielder whose ceiling is capped by the whiff rate, and whose floor is propped up by the walk rate being genuine and the hard-hit rate consistent enough to carry a projected .785 OPS without much luck required.

reports.name: Spencer Miles
reports.published_report: The xERA is 3.00 and the barrel rate is 3.8%, and those two numbers together capture what Miles actually is: a contact manager who wins by keeping the ball on the ground and out of the air, not by racking up strikeouts. His 18.3% whiff rate sits near the bottom of the league, and his 22.3% strikeout rate is right at the median, so there's no swing-and-miss carrying him. What carries him is a 6.0% walk rate that grades elite and an average exit velocity of 86.8 mph that speaks to how often he induces weak contact. The dependency is clear: if his contact suppression erodes, if hitters start squaring him up more consistently, the strikeout profile offers almost no safety net, and a 3.03 ERA gets expensive fast.

reports.name: Steven Kwan

An 8.5% whiff rate and 20.0% chase rate at the very top of the league, a 13.3% walk rate that most leadoff hitters would borrow, and yet a 0.5% barrel rate and 83.9 mph average exit velocity that both sit at the bottom of the Statcast leaderboard. The problem is getting there — a 34.4% chase rate and 31.3% whiff rate sit in the bottom fifth of the league, which is why his xBA lands at .248 despite all that raw power, and why the projection caps him at 507 PA rather than a full season. reports.name: Ketel Marte
reports.published_report: The .351 xwOBA and .278 xBA tell the same story: contact quality well above a typical middle infielder, built on a 15.0% strikeout rate that most second basemen can't touch. What makes it believable is that the underlying contact grades (.469 xSLG, 83rd percentile) aren't being propped up by a chase rate that invites pitchers to exploit him — 31.5% chase is actually below league norms. The projection's .254/.321/.451 with 25 projected home runs looks a tick conservative against those expected numbers, but the walk rate at 7.9% is a real ceiling limiter; if pitchers start working him more carefully and he doesn't draw more, the OBP stays modest and so does the offensive floor. A middle-of-the-order second baseman who makes the ball hard to get out, quietly, without the counting-stat noise that earns headlines.

Strip away the park and level inflation, and his 5.1 walks per nine become 4.7 in an MLB context — still well above where a rotation piece needs to live, and the K-BB% translates to 10.0 when MLB starters are clearing 13.5. Ninety-seven strikeouts across 96.3 innings at AAA sounds workable until you realize the swing-and-miss isn't compensating for the free passes; the 1.3 WHIP is holding together because AAA hitters aren't punishing every mistake the way MLB lineups will. If the command firms up, he's a depth arm who can eat innings without embarrassing himself; if it doesn't, the floor the profile already names is exactly where he lands.

If the power doesn't arrive, he's a bench bat who works counts well and not much more.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.published_report: The control is what makes this profile worth a second look. Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.

reports.name: Drew Cavanaugh
reports.published_report: The .449 OBP across AAA & AA is doing a lot of work here, and the BABIP of .401 is doing most of the heavy lifting behind it. Cavanaugh has 35 walks against 55 strikeouts in 227 plate appearances, which translates to an 11.4% walk rate when moved to an MLB context, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. If the average regresses hard and the power stays modest, you're left with a patient backstop who can work counts at the margin, which is a bench catcher, not a regular.

Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.

reports.name: Wilson Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is loud for a 21-year-old at A+: 58 walks across 364 plate appearances, with a translated BB% of 11.4 against a big-league pool that averages 8.5. That's the selling point. The power doesn't come with it — an ISO of .167 at A+ translates to .127 in the majors, meaningfully short of the 8.5 average, and the 20 stolen bases show he knows he has to manufacture something when he does get on. If the plate discipline holds as he climbs and the raw pop develops enough to punish pitchers for nibbling, there's a fringe regular in here; if the power stays where it is, he's a bench piece with a useful OBP, and the ceiling note in the data says the system agrees.
